area: Area I. Pilot Privileges and Currency
objective: By the end of this lesson you can tell which medical a flight needs and when it runs out, check BasicMed eligibility and limits under the current rules, and decide when a condition or medication grounds you.
why: The medical rules have changed several times since BasicMed began, and many pilots still fly on old numbers. Pilot impairment contributes to many more accidents than aircraft system failures, so the medical check belongs in every preflight [[34:182|AIM 8-1-1]].

prereading.what: Which class of medical each operation needs, when no medical is needed, the BasicMed eligibility rules in 61.23(c)(3), and the duration table in 61.23(d).
prereading.label: 14 CFR 61.23

prereading.what: The BasicMed rule itself: current aircraft, passenger, altitude, speed and logbook limits.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 61.113(i)

prereading.what: The medical education course, the comprehensive medical examination checklist (CMEC) and the special issuance conditions for BasicMed.
prereading.label: 14 CFR part 68

prereading.what: The prohibition on flying during a medical deficiency, for medical holders and for driver's license pilots.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 61.53

prereading.what: FAA guidance on BasicMed. Useful background, but its occupant, passenger, weight and safety pilot lines are out of date.
prereading.label: AC 68-1A, 3-1 to 5-4

prereading.what: Fitness for flight: illness, medication, alcohol, fatigue, stress, emotion and the personal checklist.
prereading.label: AIM 8-1-1

prereading.what: Alcohol and drugs, with the 48-hour and five-dosing-interval rules of thumb.
prereading.label: PHAK 17-15 to 17-18

warmup: Your FAA medical ran out last month, but you feel great and only fly on weekends. How might you still be legal to act as PIC tomorrow, and what could ground you even with a brand-new medical?

key_terms.def: First, second or third class, issued under 14 CFR part 67. The class you need depends on the privileges you use.
Aviation Medical Examiner: a physician trained in aviation medicine who does FAA medical exams.
Runs to the last day of the month. Medical and BasicMed periods end at the end of a month, not on the exam date.
Flying under 14 CFR 61.113(i) without an FAA medical, using a U.S. driver's license, a medical course and a physician's exam.
Comprehensive Medical Examination Checklist: you fill in your part, a state-licensed physician examines you and signs it.
FAA-accepted online BasicMed course under 14 CFR 68.3, taken every 24 calendar months.
An FAA medical issued at the FAA's discretion to a pilot with a disqualifying condition, after special testing.
A condition, medication or treatment that makes you unable to meet your medical standard or to fly safely (14 CFR 61.53).
A pilot the aircraft or a rule requires on board, such as a safety pilot during simulated instrument flight.
Self-check before flight: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion.
The time between recommended or prescribed doses of a medication.

chunks.title: Which medical does the flight need?

body.p: 14 CFR 61.23(a) ties the medical to the privileges you use on that flight, not to the certificate in your wallet [[60:204|14 CFR 61.23(a)]].

head: Medical
You need it when you...
Rule
rows: Act as PIC using ATP privileges; act as SIC using ATP privileges in a part 121 flag or supplemental operation that needs three or more pilots; serve as a required pilot in part 121 after your 60th birthday
Act as SIC using ATP privileges in other part 121 operations; use commercial pilot privileges in an airplane
At least third class, or BasicMed
Use student, recreational or private privileges; act as PIC or required pilot as a flight instructor; take a practical test in an aircraft; act as an examiner in an aircraft

body.p: A higher class covers the lower ones. Because the class only matters for the privileges you use, a first class works for commercial and private flying once it no longer covers ATP flying [[1:424|PHAK 17-2]].

callout.text: Match the medical to the flight: ATP captain = first, paid flying = second, private flying = third or BasicMed.
Common mistake: an airline or commercial pilot whose medical lapsed for that job thinks they are grounded from everything. The same certificate often still covers private flying [[1:424|PHAK 17-2]].

check.q: You hold an ATP and a valid second class. You'll fly your own airplane to visit family, no pay. Which medical does that flight need?
check.a: Third class or BasicMed. You are using private privileges [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23(a)(3)(i)]].

chunks.title: No medical needed, and what to carry

body.p: Some flying needs no medical at all [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23(b)]]:

bullets: A flight instructor who is not acting as PIC or as a required pilot [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23(b)(7)]].
A ground instructor [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23(b)(8)]].
A practical test or proficiency check in a flight simulator or flight training device [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23(b)(10)]].
Glider flying, and balloon flying under a private certificate [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23(b)(3)-(4)]].

body.p: A sport pilot may use either an FAA medical or a U.S. driver's license, in aircraft that meet the 61.316 limits [[60:206|14 CFR 61.23(c)(1)(ii)]].

**Carry it.** A required pilot must hold the medical (or other documentation the FAA accepts) in physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(c)(1)]]. Under BasicMed, a U.S. driver's license takes its place [[60:190|14 CFR 61.3(c)(2)(xiii)]], and it must be in your personal possession when you fly [[36:10|AC 68-1A 4.2]]. You also need photo ID [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(2)]].

callout.text: Flight review or IPC: if you act as PIC, your instructor needs no medical [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23(b)(7)]]. If you can't act as PIC, the instructor must, and then needs at least a third class or BasicMed [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23(a)(3)(ii)]] [[60:206|14 CFR 61.23(c)(1)(vii)]].

check.q: Your CFI's medical has expired. Can she give you a flight review while you act as PIC?
check.a: Yes. A flight instructor who is not acting as PIC or required pilot needs no medical [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23(b)(7)]].

body.p: A medical expires at the end of the last day of a month, counted from the month of the exam date shown on it. Your age on the exam date sets the length [[60:208|14 CFR 61.23(d)]].

head: Privileges used
Under 40 at exam
40 or older at exam
Rule
rows: ATP PIC, or ATP SIC in a 3-pilot flag or supplemental operation (first class)
Commercial, or other part 121 ATP SIC (first or second class)
Private, recreational, student, CFI as PIC (any class)

body.p: Example: you are 52 and pass a first class exam on January 15, 2026. It covers ATP PIC flying through July 31, 2026, commercial flying through January 31, 2027, and private flying through January 31, 2028 [[60:208|14 CFR 61.23(d)(1)]] [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(1)(v)]].

callout.text: Calendar months run to the end of the month. A 24 calendar month period that starts July 15, 2016 runs until July 31, 2018 [[36:7|AC 68-1A 2.3]].

Common mistake: PHAK 17-2 says a first class lasts one year "if the airman is 40 or younger" [[1:424|PHAK 17-2]]. The rule says under age 40 on the exam date. At exactly 40 you get 6 months for ATP PIC flying [[60:208|14 CFR 61.23(d)(1)(ii)]].

check.q: You were 39 at your third class exam on May 3, 2024. When does it run out for private flying?
check.a: At the end of May 31, 2029: the 60th month after May 2024 [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(3)(i)]].

chunks.title: BasicMed: who can use it and what you need

body.p: The rule reads: "A private pilot may act as pilot in command or serve as a required flightcrew member of an aircraft without holding a medical certificate" if the pilot holds a valid U.S. driver's license, meets 61.23(c)(3) and keeps to the limits [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)]]. It also covers student and recreational pilots [[60:206|14 CFR 61.23(c)(1)(v)]] and flight instructors acting as PIC or required crew [[60:206|14 CFR 61.23(c)(1)(vii)]].

head: You need
Rule
In practice
rows: A valid U.S. driver's license, and you follow its medical restrictions
A passport or foreign license does not count, and limits such as daylight driving only apply to your flying [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.2]] [[36:10|AC 68-1A 4.2]]
An FAA medical held at any time after July 14, 2006

It may be expired or a special issuance. It may not have been suspended or revoked, your last special issuance may not have been withdrawn, and your last application may not have been completed and denied [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)(ii)-(iv)]]
The medical education course within the last 24 calendar months
Keep the completion certificate in your logbook [[60:405|14 CFR 68.3(b)(1)]]
A comprehensive medical exam by a state-licensed physician within the last 48 calendar months, done with the CMEC
The physician does not need to be an AME [[36:19|AC 68-1A 7.1]]
Care and treatment by a physician for any diagnosed condition that may affect your flying
You certify this in the course [[60:405|14 CFR 68.3(b)(3)]]

body.p: **The exam.** You fill in your part of the CMEC and give it to the physician [[60:405|14 CFR 68.5(a)]]. The physician checks every listed item, discusses every drug you take, and signs that they know of no condition that, as presently treated, could interfere with safe flight [[60:407|14 CFR 68.7(c)(3)-(4)]].
**Your logbook** must hold the completed CMEC and the course completion certificate [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(3)]]. You don't need papers proving the old FAA medical [[36:12|AC 68-1A 4.3.2.3]].

callout.text: Changed: AC 68-1A says the exam must be within "the past 48 months" and applies the course, exam and physician-care rules to the PIC only [[36:8|AC 68-1A 3.3]] [[36:12|AC 68-1A 4.4-4.6]]. The current rule says 48 calendar months, and applies to the PIC or any required flightcrew member [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)(i)(C)-(E)]].

Common mistake: applying for a new FAA medical "just to see." Once the AME opens your application it is in process. If it ends completed and denied, you can't use BasicMed, even while you appeal [[36:11|AC 68-1A 4.3.2.1]].

check.q: Your last medical expired in 2019 and was never suspended. Can it count toward BasicMed?
check.a: Yes. It may be expired. It only has to have been held after July 14, 2006 and not suspended, revoked or denied [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)]].

body.p: These are the limits as 14 CFR 61.113(i) reads now [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)-(2)]]:

head: Limit
Current rule
rows: Authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)]]
No more than 6 on board [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)]]
Maximum takeoff weight not more than 12,500 lb [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)]]
Not more than 18,000 ft MSL on any part of the flight [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(2)(i)]]
Not more than 250 knots indicated airspeed [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(2)(iii)]]
Inside the United States, unless the country you fly in authorizes it [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(2)(ii)]]

body.p: Class A airspace starts at 18,000 ft MSL [[1:377|PHAK 15-2]], so BasicMed keeps you out of the flight levels above it. The limits cover the whole flight, takeoff to full-stop landing. If the BasicMed pilot is PIC, no part of the flight may go past them, even if another pilot aboard holds a medical [[36:16|AC 68-1A 5.2.5]].

**IFR is fine.** You still need an instrument rating, IFR currency and an airplane approved for IFR [[36:14|AC 68-1A 5.2.3]]. If forecast icing or storms on your route could force you above 18,000 ft, the FAA considers starting that flight contrary to BasicMed [[36:15|AC 68-1A 5.2.4.2]].

**No pay.** BasicMed gives private-pilot privileges, so the private limits apply, with exceptions such as sharing costs pro rata [[60:307|14 CFR 61.113(a)]] [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(c)]]. Commercial privileges need at least a second class [[60:204|14 CFR 61.23(a)(2)(ii)]] [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.1.2]].

callout.text: Changed: AC 68-1A still says 6 occupants, 5 passengers and 6,000 lb [[36:8|AC 68-1A 3.2]] [[36:13|AC 68-1A 5.1.1]], and 6 occupants for experimental aircraft [[36:13|AC 68-1A 5.1.3]]. The current rules allow 7 occupants, 6 passengers and 12,500 lb [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)]] [[60:512|14 CFR 91.319(j)]]. AC 5.2.4 also uses old paragraph numbers: it lists compensation as 61.113(i)(2)(i) and airspeed as (2)(iv) [[36:15|AC 68-1A 5.2.4.1]] [[36:16|AC 68-1A 5.2.4.4]]. Today (2)(i) is altitude, (2)(ii) is outside the U.S. and (2)(iii) is airspeed [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(2)]].

check.q: BasicMed PIC, 6-seat airplane, 5 friends aboard. You plan to cruise at 19,000 ft to stay above the weather. Legal?
check.a: No. No part of the flight may be above 18,000 ft MSL [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(2)(i)]].

bullets: **Safety pilot.** A safety pilot is a required flightcrew member [[36:14|AC 68-1A 5.2.2.1]] and needs at least a private certificate with the right category and class [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)]]. The current rule lets a BasicMed pilot "serve as a required flightcrew member" [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)]], so a BasicMed pilot may be your safety pilot.

**Flight instructors.** A CFI acting as PIC may use BasicMed [[60:206|14 CFR 61.23(c)(1)(vii)]]. A CFI paid for instruction while acting as PIC is exercising only private pilot privileges [[36:14|AC 68-1A 5.2.2.2]].
**Examiners.** An examiner may now give a test or check in an aircraft under 61.113(i) [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23(a)(3)(iv)]] [[60:206|14 CFR 61.23(c)(1)(viii)]].
**Student pilots.** Where the student limits of 61.89 conflict with 61.113(i), the student follows 61.89 [[60:279|14 CFR 61.89(d)]].

callout.text: Changed: AC 68-1A says BasicMed can't be used to fly as a safety pilot unless that pilot is PIC, and that it covers no one but the PIC [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.1]] [[36:14|AC 68-1A 5.2.2.1]]. It also says examiners can't use BasicMed [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.1.3]]. Both are outdated.

body.p: **Special issuance first.** For these diagnoses you must finish the FAA special issuance process before using BasicMed [[60:407|14 CFR 68.9(a)]] [[60:408|14 CFR 68.9(a)]]:

head: Group
Conditions
rows: Personality disorder shown by repeated overt acts, psychosis, bipolar disorder, substance dependence in the last 2 years [[60:407|14 CFR 68.9(a)(1)]] [[60:408|14 CFR 68.9(a)(1)]]
Epilepsy; disturbance of consciousness or transient loss of nervous system control without a satisfactory explanation [[60:408|14 CFR 68.9(a)(2)]]
Heart (one-time special issuance for each diagnosis)
Heart attack, coronary heart disease that needed treatment, heart valve replacement, heart replacement [[60:408|14 CFR 68.9(a)(3)]]

body.p: With a diagnosed mental health or neurological condition, BasicMed doesn't apply if your specialist judges you unable to fly safely, or if your driver's license was revoked for that condition. You also certify every 2 years that you are under a specialist's care [[60:408|14 CFR 68.9(c)-(d)]] [[60:409|14 CFR 68.9(d)]]. The FAA can ask for more information if it gets credible reports, for example from the National Driver Register [[60:409|14 CFR 68.11]].

check.q: You had a heart valve replacement 3 years ago and have never applied for a special issuance. Can you go straight to BasicMed?
check.a: No. First complete the special issuance process, once, for that diagnosis [[60:408|14 CFR 68.9(a)(3)]].

body.p: A medical certificate shows you met the standards on exam day. 14 CFR 61.53 decides whether you may fly today [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53]].

head: How you are qualified
You may not act as PIC or required pilot while you...
Rule
rows: Know or have reason to know of a condition, or take medication or treatment, that makes you unable to meet the standards for the medical the flight needs
Know or have reason to know of a condition that makes you unable to fly the aircraft safely

body.p: BasicMed pilots sign this in the course: "I understand that I cannot act as pilot in command, or any other capacity as a required flight crew member, if I know or have reason to know of any medical condition that would make me unable to operate the aircraft in a safe manner." [[60:405|14 CFR 68.3(b)(5)]]

**Alcohol and drugs.** No crewmember may act within 8 hours of drinking any alcohol, while under the influence, while using any drug that affects the faculties in any way contrary to safety, or with an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or more [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]].

Eight hours is the legal minimum, not a safe number. As little as one beer can impair flying skills, and the AIM suggests 12 to 24 hours from bottle to throttle [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]]. The body needs about 3 hours to clear one drink, and with a hangover you are still under the influence [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

callout.text: Common mistake: "8 hours and I'm legal." If you are at 0.04 or more after 8 hours, you still can't fly. If you are well below 0.04, you still need the full 8 hours [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

check.q: You fly under BasicMed. Which 61.53 standard applies to you?
check.a: 61.53(b), through 61.53(c)(2): don't fly if you know or have reason to know of a condition that makes you unable to fly safely [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(c)]].

chunks.title: Medications: over the counter and prescription

body.p: No regulation lists which drugs are allowed. The two rules to remember are 61.53 and 91.17 [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].

bullets: Tranquilizers, sedatives, strong pain relievers and cough suppressants can impair judgment, memory, alertness, coordination and vision [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]].
Antihistamines, blood pressure drugs, muscle relaxants and medicines for diarrhea or motion sickness have side effects that impair the same functions [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]].
Diphenhydramine (for example Benadryl) causes drowsiness and stays in your body a long time [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].
Nervous system depressants make you more prone to hypoxia [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]].
The condition behind the medicine may itself be disqualifying [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].
The FAA says marijuana use by airmen is prohibited [[1:439|PHAK 17-17]].

head: Situation
Rule of thumb
rows: Any new medication, over the counter or prescribed
Wait at least 48 hours after the first dose to see whether it affects you [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]
A medication with sedating or dizzying side effects
Wait five maximal dosing intervals. A 5 to 6 hour interval means 30 hours [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]
Talk to an AME before you fly [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]

body.p: The safest rule is not to fly as a crewmember while taking any medication, unless the FAA has approved it [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]].

callout.text: BasicMed: the physician must discuss every drug you report, prescription or not [[60:407|14 CFR 68.7(c)(3)]]. Bring a full list, supplements too [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].

check.q: You took a sedating allergy pill whose label gives a 6-hour dosing interval. Rule-of-thumb wait before flying?

chunks.title: Risk: legal on paper, unsafe today

body.p: Pilot impairment contributes to many more accidents than aircraft system failures, so do a preflight check on yourself as well as the airplane [[34:182|AIM 8-1-1]]. A valid medical or current BasicMed papers can't tell you how you feel this morning.

head: IMSAFE item
What to look for
rows: Even a minor illness can hurt judgment, memory and alertness. Safest rule: don't fly with any illness [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]]
Prescription and over-the-counter drugs both have side effects [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]
Can lead you to press on into bad weather to keep a schedule. Consider delaying [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]]
Hangover and dehydration can last past 8 hours [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]
Often not noticed until serious errors are made. Sleep apnea robs you of restful sleep; get checked if you have its symptoms [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]]
After a serious argument, a death in the family, divorce or job loss, don't fly until you have recovered [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]] [[34:182|AIM 8-1-1]]

body.p: Stress is not on the regulations' list of grounding conditions, but you still have to weigh it [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]]. External pressure is how pilots talk themselves into flying sick. Allow extra time, have a backup plan, tell people you might be late, and carry an overnight kit with your prescriptions [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].

callout.text: Ask "Can I meet the standard today?" not "Is my medical current?" A known condition or treatment grounds you whatever the date on the card [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(a)]].

check.q: Your medical is current, but your father died two days ago and you slept badly. What does the AIM say?
check.a: Don't fly until you have recovered from an emotionally upsetting event, and watch fatigue too [[34:182|AIM 8-1-1]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: the medical go/no-go check

body.p: Run this before every flight review, every passenger trip and any flight where your health has changed:

bullets: 1. **Class.** Which privileges will I use on this flight? Pick the medical [[60:204|14 CFR 61.23(a)]].
2. **Clock.** FAA medical: is it current for that class, using my age on the exam date and counting to the end of the month [[60:208|14 CFR 61.23(d)]]?

3. **BasicMed papers.** U.S. driver's license, course within 24 calendar months, CMEC exam within 48 calendar months [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)]], and both documents in my logbook [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(3)]].
4. **BasicMed limits.** 7 occupants, 6 passengers, 12,500 lb, 18,000 ft MSL, 250 KIAS, inside the U.S., no paid flying [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)]] [[60:307|14 CFR 61.113(a)]].
5. **Carry.** Medical or driver's license, plus photo ID, on me [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(c)(1)]] [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(2)]].
6. **Conditions.** Any new diagnosis, medicine or treatment since my exam [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53]]? Any condition that needs a special issuance under BasicMed [[60:407|14 CFR 68.9]]?
7. **Today.** Alcohol: 8 hours and under 0.04 at the very least; no drug that affects me [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]]. Then IMSAFE [[34:182|AIM 8-1-1]].

callout.text: Class, clock, papers, limits, carry, conditions, today.

check.q: Step 1 says you'll use private privileges and you're on BasicMed. What's the next thing to check?
check.a: Your BasicMed papers: driver's license, course within 24 calendar months, exam within 48, and the CMEC and certificate in your logbook [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)]] [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(3)]].

bullets: Using AC 68-1A's old limits of 6 occupants, 5 passengers and 6,000 lb [[36:8|AC 68-1A 3.2]]. Now: 7, 6 and 12,500 lb [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)]].
Thinking a BasicMed pilot can't be a safety pilot [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)]].
Thinking a lapsed medical ends all flying, when it may still cover lower privileges [[1:424|PHAK 17-2]].
Counting from the exam date instead of to the end of the month, or using today's age instead of age at the exam [[60:208|14 CFR 61.23(d)]].
Applying for an FAA medical, being denied, and finding BasicMed is closed too [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)(iv)]].
Believing BasicMed allows paid flying for a commercial pilot [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.1.2]].
Leaving the CMEC and course certificate out of the logbook [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(3)]].

Reading AIM 8-1-1's line that all pilots except glider and balloon pilots must hold a medical [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]] as the whole story. BasicMed and sport pilots may use a driver's license [[60:206|14 CFR 61.23(c)(1)]].
Flying the same day you start a new medicine [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

check.q: Why is AIM 8-1-1's statement that all pilots except glider and balloon pilots need a medical incomplete?
check.a: Current 61.23(c) lets sport pilots and BasicMed pilots fly with a U.S. driver's license instead [[60:206|14 CFR 61.23(c)(1)]].

Each line starts with a red letter: Illness, do I have any symptoms; Medication, have I been taking prescription or over-the-counter drugs; Stress, am I under psychological pressure from the job, worried about money, health or family; Alcohol, have I been drinking within 8 hours, within 24 hours; Fatigue, am I tired and not adequately rested; Emotion, am I emotionally upset.

f2.caption: Figure 17-8. Impairment scale with alcohol use.
f2.alt: Blue table. Top part lists typical servings and pure alcohol content: table wine 4 oz, light beer 12 oz, champagne 4 oz each about .48 oz; aperitif 1.5 oz .38; vodka 1 oz and whiskey 1.25 oz .50. Lower part lists blood alcohol ranges and effects, from 0.01 to 0.05 percent where a person appears normal, through impaired judgment and reaction time at 0.03 to 0.12, up to unconsciousness and possible death at 0.35 to 0.50. A footnote says the legal driving limit in most states is 0.08 or 0.10 percent.

f3.caption: Figure 17-9. Adverse affects of various drugs.
f3.alt: Table with columns Substance, Generic or Brand Name, Treatment for, and Possible Side Effects. Rows: alcohol, nicotine, amphetamines, caffeine, antacids, antihistamines (such as Contac, Dristan, Dimetapp, diphenhydramine, for allergies and colds, causing drowsiness, dizziness and visual disturbances) and aspirin, each with its side effects listed.

f4.alt: Four green panels: Pilot, Aircraft, Environment and External pressures. The Pilot panel describes a pilot with a few hours of sleep and the start of a cold, and another with 4 hours of sleep who declines a flight his boss wanted. The External pressures panel tells of a ferry pilot who stretched fuel to keep a schedule.

f5.alt: Cutaway of U.S. airspace. A red Class A band runs from 18,000 ft MSL up to FL 600 over the top. Below it, blue Class E surrounds the yellow Class B wedding cake, green Class C and orange Class D cylinders, with pink Class G near the ground and up to 14,500 ft MSL on the left.

scenario.title: A wedding, a cold and a new prescription
scenario.setup: You are a 58-year-old private pilot, instrument rated, flying under BasicMed. You took the online course 14 months ago and had your CMEC exam with your family doctor 3 years ago. On Saturday you plan to fly your spouse and two friends 280 NM to a family wedding in a 4-seat single. On Thursday at 2000 you took the first dose of a new blood pressure prescription. Friday you come down with a cold. Friday dinner you have two glasses of wine, the last at 2100, and at 2300 you take a nighttime cold medicine with diphenhydramine; its label gives a 6-hour dosing interval. Departure is planned for 0700 Saturday.

questions.q: Do your BasicMed papers and the airplane fit this flight?
questions.a: Yes, on paper. The course is within 24 calendar months and the exam within 48 [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)(i)(C)-(D)]]. Three passengers in a 4-seat airplane is well inside 6 passengers and 7 occupants [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)]]. Make sure the CMEC and course certificate are in your logbook [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(3)]], and that a physician is treating your blood pressure [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)(i)(E)]].

questions.q: The last glass of wine was at 2100. Are you legal at 0700, and is it smart?
questions.a: That is 10 hours, so you meet the 8-hour rule if you are also below 0.04 and not under the influence [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]]. The AIM suggests 12 to 24 hours, and alcohol also makes you more prone to disorientation and hypoxia [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]].

questions.q: What about the cold medicine taken at 2300?
questions.a: Only 8 hours will have passed. Diphenhydramine causes drowsiness and lasts a long time [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]]. With a 6-hour dosing interval, the five-interval rule of thumb means 30 hours, so not before about 0500 Sunday [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]. Flying on it would also break 91.17(a)(3) if it affects your faculties [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(3)]].

questions.q: And the new blood pressure pill?
questions.a: The first dose was Thursday at 2000. The 48-hour rule of thumb runs to Saturday at 2000, so 0700 Saturday is too soon [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]. Blood pressure drugs have side effects that can impair you [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]].

questions.q: Which legal standard decides whether you may act as PIC, and what is the answer?
questions.a: As a driver's license pilot you follow 61.53(b): you may not act as PIC if you know or have reason to know of a condition that makes you unable to fly safely [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(b)-(c)]]. You signed that statement in the course [[60:405|14 CFR 68.3(b)(5)]]. With a cold, two new medicines and a short night, the answer is no-go [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]].

questions.q: The wedding is a must-attend event. How do you handle the pressure?
questions.a: Plan for it: leave a day early next time, or have a backup such as driving or an airline ticket, and tell the family you may arrive late [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]]. The key is to be ready for and accept delays [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].

skills.do: Given a pilot's certificate, medical status (FAA medical or BasicMed), health and planned flight, decide whether the pilot may act as PIC, and name the rule: 61.23 for the class and duration, 61.113(i) and 61.23(c)(3) for BasicMed, and 61.53 and 91.17 for fitness today.
skills.practice: Before your flight review, run the go/no-go check in chunk 10 on your own documents and show your instructor your medical or your logbook with the CMEC and course certificate [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(3)]]. The flight review guide includes 91.17 and fitness for flight in its regulatory review [[15:40|AC 61-98E App E]] [[15:43|AC 61-98E App F]].

quiz.q: A commercial pilot will be paid to fly a pipeline patrol in an airplane. What is the minimum medical?
options: Third class
First class
Second class
BasicMed is enough
quiz.why: Commercial privileges in an airplane need at least a second class [[60:204|14 CFR 61.23(a)(2)(ii)]]. BasicMed does not cover commercial privileges [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.1.2]].

quiz.q: You were 45 at your third class exam on April 8, 2025. When does it run out for private flying?
options: End of April 30, 2027
April 8, 2027
End of April 30, 2030
End of April 30, 2026
quiz.why: Age 40 or older: the 24th month after the exam month, to the end of that month [[60:210|14 CFR 61.23(d)(3)(ii)]]. 60 months is for pilots under 40.

quiz.q: Under the current BasicMed rule, how many passengers may you carry?
quiz.why: No more than 6 passengers, in an aircraft authorized for not more than 7 occupants [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)]]. The 5 in AC 68-1A is outdated [[36:8|AC 68-1A 3.2]].

quiz.q: How often must a BasicMed pilot complete the medical education course?
options: Every 12 calendar months
Every 24 calendar months
Every 48 calendar months
Every 60 calendar months
quiz.why: The course must be completed within the 24 calendar months before you fly under 61.113(i) [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)(i)(C)]]. The exam is the 48-month item.

quiz.q: Which of these can NOT be used to meet the BasicMed driver's license requirement?
options: A U.S. state driver's license with a corrective lenses restriction
A current U.S. state driver's license with no restrictions
A U.S. driver's license limited to daylight driving
An official U.S. passport
quiz.why: A passport works as photo ID but can't replace the driver's license for BasicMed. Restricted U.S. licenses count, but their restrictions also apply to your flying [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.2]] [[36:10|AC 68-1A 4.2]].

quiz.q: A pilot with a valid FAA medical learns of a condition that keeps them from meeting its standards. Under 61.53(a), what may they do?
options: Fly until the certificate expires
Fly, and report it at the next exam
Fly solo only, with no passengers
Not act as PIC or as a required pilot
quiz.why: No one may act as PIC or required pilot while knowing or having reason to know of such a condition [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(a)(1)]].

quiz.q: What is the regulatory minimum time between drinking alcohol and acting as a crewmember?
options: 4 hours
12 hours
8 hours
24 hours
quiz.why: No one may act as a crewmember within 8 hours after drinking any alcohol [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(1)]]. 12 to 24 hours is the AIM's advice, not the rule [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]].

quiz.q: A BasicMed pilot wants to fly to the Bahamas. What does the rule say?
options: Only if that country authorizes it
Always allowed, since FAA certificates meet ICAO standards
Allowed if you stay under 250 KIAS
Allowed only under VFR
quiz.why: No part of the flight may be outside the United States unless the country you fly in authorizes it [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(2)(ii)]]. BasicMed differs from ICAO standards [[36:15|AC 68-1A 5.2.4.3]].

quiz.q: Which diagnosis needs the special issuance process before you may use BasicMed?
options: Seasonal allergies treated with an antihistamine
Coronary heart disease that needed treatment
A kidney stone that passed years ago, without surgery
Wearing glasses or contacts for vision
quiz.why: Treated coronary heart disease is on the 68.9 list and needs a one-time special issuance [[60:408|14 CFR 68.9(a)(3)(ii)]].

quiz.q: By the PHAK rule of thumb, how long after the first dose of a new medication should you wait before flying?
options: 8 hours
24 hours
48 hours
72 hours
quiz.why: Wait at least 48 hours after the first dose to make sure there are no side effects that make flying unsafe [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

takeaways: Pick the medical by the privileges you use: ATP captain first class, paid flying second class, private flying third class or BasicMed.
Medicals end at the end of a month. Your age on the exam date sets 6, 12, 24 or 60 months, and the certificate then drops to lower privileges.
BasicMed: U.S. driver's license, an FAA medical held after July 14, 2006, the course every 24 calendar months, the CMEC exam every 48, both in your logbook.
BasicMed limits now: 7 occupants, 6 passengers, 12,500 lb, 18,000 ft MSL, 250 KIAS, inside the U.S., no paid flying. Ignore AC 68-1A's older numbers.
A BasicMed pilot may now serve as a required flightcrew member, such as a safety pilot.
61.53 grounds you for a known condition or medication, whatever the date on your medical. 8 hours and under 0.04 is only the legal minimum.
Wait 48 hours on a new medicine and five dosing intervals on a sedating one, and run IMSAFE before every flight.
cfi_notes: AC 68-1A (5/3/17) is out of date on several lines. Teach the current 14 CFR: 7 occupants, 6 passengers and 12,500 lb, not 6, 5 and 6,000 lb (AC 3.2, 5.1.1, 5.2.1) [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)]]; 7 occupants for experimental aircraft, not 6 (AC 5.1.3) [[60:512|14 CFR 91.319(j)]].

Also outdated in AC 68-1A: BasicMed is no longer PIC-only, so a BasicMed pilot may be a safety pilot (AC 4.1, 4.4 to 4.6, 5.2.2.1); examiners may use it (AC 4.1.3); the exam period is now 48 calendar months (AC 3.3, 4.6, 7.1 say 48 months); and AC 5.2.4 cites paragraph numbers that no longer match 61.113(i)(2) [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)]] [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23(a)(3)(iv)]].
PHAK 17-2 says a first class lasts a year "if the airman is 40 or younger" and does not mention BasicMed [[1:424|PHAK 17-2]]. The rule is under age 40 on the exam date [[60:208|14 CFR 61.23(d)(1)]].

AIM 8-1-1.a.1 still says all pilots except glider and balloon pilots must hold a medical [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]]. Point out that sport and BasicMed pilots may use a driver's license under 61.23(c) [[60:206|14 CFR 61.23(c)(1)]].

Experienced pilots most often miss the end-of-month rule, age at exam versus age today, and that a lapsed first or second class still covers private flying. Have them work their own certificate's dates out loud.

Ask BasicMed pilots to show the CMEC and course certificate in their logbook during the flight review; the AC 61-98E guide lists 91.17 and fitness for flight for the regulatory review [[15:40|AC 61-98E App E]].
Probe 61.53 with a real example: a cold, a new prescription, a sleepless night. The answer to "is it legal?" and "is it safe?" should both be no [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53]] [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]].
Warn pilots on BasicMed that applying for an FAA medical and being denied ends BasicMed eligibility, even during an appeal [[36:11|AC 68-1A 4.3.2.1]].
gaps: No uploaded advisory circular reflects the BasicMed changes (7 occupants, 12,500 lb, required flightcrew members, examiners); AC 68-1A dates from 5/3/17, so the lesson relies on the current 14 CFR text and flags the AC 68-1A lines.
The FAA Do Not Issue / Do Not Fly medication list and the AME Guide, named in AC 68-1A 2.2.3, are not in the uploaded sources; medication guidance here comes from PHAK Ch 17 and AIM 8-1-1.
The part 67 medical standards themselves (vision, hearing, blood pressure limits) are outside this lesson; only the disqualifying conditions listed in PHAK 17-2 and 14 CFR 68.9 are taught.
AC 68-1A Appendix A (the CMEC form) is a scanned image in the source and can't be quoted; the checklist items come from 14 CFR 68.7.
Sport pilot rules, including the new night sport pilot operations under 61.113(i) in 14 CFR 61.23(c)(1)(vi), are only mentioned, not taught.
No source gives dosing intervals for specific drugs such as diphenhydramine; pilots must read the label or ask an AME.

activities.title: Which medical does this flight need?
activities.intro: Tap a flight, then the medical it needs.

pairs.r: At least a second class medical

pairs.l: CFI giving a review, not PIC

pairs.r: A U.S. driver's license or an FAA medical

activities.title: When does it run out?
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: You are 52 and pass a first class exam on January 15, 2026. Your ATP PIC privileges last through the end of which month of 2026? Type the month number (January = 1).
items.why: Age 40 or older: ATP PIC privileges last to the end of the 6th month after the exam month. January + 6 = July, so through July 31, 2026 [[60:208|14 CFR 61.23(d)(1)(ii)]].

items.q: Same certificate (age 52, exam January 15, 2026). It covers private pilot flying through the end of January of which year?
items.why: Age 40 or older, private privileges: 24th month after the exam month. January 2026 + 24 months = January 2028 [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(1)(v)]].

items.q: You are 47 and pass a second class exam on March 5, 2026. It covers commercial flying through the end of which month of 2027? Type the month number.
items.why: Commercial privileges: 12th month after the exam month at any age. March 2026 + 12 months = March 2027, so through March 31, 2027 [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(2)(i)]].

items.q: You are 33 and pass a third class exam on October 2, 2025. It covers private flying through the end of October of which year?
items.why: Under 40: 60th month after the exam month. October 2025 + 60 months = October 2030 [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(3)(i)]].

activities.title: Getting onto BasicMed
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Fill in your section of the CMEC
Give the completed CMEC to a state-licensed physician
The physician examines you, discusses your medicines and signs the CMEC
Take the online course and enter the physician's details and exam date
Keep the course certificate and the CMEC in your logbook
Act as PIC within the BasicMed limits

activities.title: True or false: BasicMed limits today
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Under the current rule, a BasicMed pilot may carry 6 passengers.
cards.why: True. The aircraft may be authorized for up to 7 occupants with no more than 6 passengers [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)]].

cards.s: An airplane with an 8,000 lb maximum takeoff weight is too heavy for BasicMed.
cards.why: False. The current limit is 12,500 lb [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)]]. The 6,000 lb figure in AC 68-1A is outdated [[36:13|AC 68-1A 5.1.1]].

cards.s: An instrument-rated, current BasicMed pilot may fly IFR in clouds.
cards.why: True. BasicMed allows IFR and IMC, but you still need the rating, currency and an IFR-approved airplane [[36:14|AC 68-1A 5.2.3]].

cards.s: The 250-knot BasicMed limit is a true airspeed limit.
cards.why: False. It is indicated airspeed: no part of the flight above 250 knots indicated [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(2)(iii)]].

cards.s: If a pilot aboard holds a first class, the BasicMed PIC may climb above 18,000 ft for part of the trip.
cards.why: False. When the BasicMed pilot is PIC, the limits apply to the entire flight [[36:16|AC 68-1A 5.2.5]] [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(2)(i)]].

cards.s: An experimental airplane flown under BasicMed may carry 7 occupants.
cards.why: True. 91.319(j) now allows not more than 7 occupants [[60:512|14 CFR 91.319(j)]].

activities.title: BasicMed: yes or not yet?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs. Assume each pilot has a U.S. driver's license, a current course and a CMEC exam, unless the clue says otherwise.

items.t: Last FAA medical expired in 2015, never suspended
Most recent medical application completed and denied
Heart attack last year, no special issuance yet
Last medical was a special issuance that simply expired
Driver's license revoked and not yet reinstated
Treated high blood pressure, under a doctor's care
Last medical was suspended, then expired while suspended

activities.title: Timing checks: meds, alcohol, BasicMed
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: A sedating medicine has a maximum dosing interval of 8 hours. Using the PHAK rule of thumb, how many hours after your last dose should you wait before flying?
items.why: Wait five maximal dosing intervals: 5 x 8 = 40 hours [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

items.q: You take the first dose of a new prescription Monday at 1900. Under the 48-hour rule of thumb, what hour on Wednesday is the earliest you should fly? (24-hour clock, for example 1900 = 19)
Your last drink was at 2200. Assuming you are well below 0.04, what is the earliest hour the next morning you may act as a crewmember? (24-hour clock)
items.why: 91.17 requires 8 hours after any alcohol: 2200 + 8 hours = 0600 [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(1)]]. The AIM suggests waiting 12 to 24 hours [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]].

items.q: You completed the BasicMed course on June 5, 2025. It stays valid through the end of June of which year?
items.why: The course must be within the 24 calendar months before you fly [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)(i)(C)]]. June 2025 + 24 calendar months runs to June 30, 2027 [[36:7|AC 68-1A 2.3]].

activities.title: Can I take this flight?
activities.intro: You hold a commercial pilot certificate with an instrument rating. Your last FAA medical, a second class from 2022, has expired. It was never suspended and you haven't applied since. You had your BasicMed exam with your family doctor 30 months ago and took the online course 26 months ago. Next Saturday you plan to fly five friends in your turbocharged six-seat single.

steps.s: First, check your BasicMed status. What is true?
options: You're good to go: BasicMed is current
Get a new BasicMed exam first: it's more than 24 months old
Retake the online course first: it's more than 24 calendar months old
You need a new FAA medical, because your old one expired
steps.why: The course must be within 24 calendar months; the exam has 48 [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)(i)(C)-(D)]]. An expired medical is fine for BasicMed [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)(ii)(B)]].

steps.s: You retake the course on Monday. One friend offers you $300 for flying them. What do you do?
options: Accept: you hold a commercial certificate, so flying for pay is within your privileges
Accept, as long as you file IFR and keep the flight within the BasicMed limits
Accept, because carrying five passengers is inside the BasicMed passenger limits
Decline the pay; you may share fuel, oil, airport and rental costs pro rata
steps.why: Commercial privileges need at least a second class [[60:204|14 CFR 61.23(a)(2)(ii)]]. Under BasicMed you use private privileges, and you may pay no less than your pro rata share [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(c)]].

steps.s: Thursday's forecast shows icing in clouds with tops near 19,000 ft along your route. Your airplane can climb to 20,000 ft. Your plan?
options: File for 20,000 ft to stay on top of the icing, since your airplane can climb that high
Go, and let a friend with a first class take over as PIC for the climb above 18,000 ft
Go, and climb above 18,000 ft only if you pick up ice, then descend once clear of it
Plan a route and altitude at or below 18,000 ft that avoids the icing, or delay
steps.why: No part of the flight may be above 18,000 ft MSL [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(2)(i)]]. Starting a flight when forecast weather may force you higher is contrary to BasicMed [[36:15|AC 68-1A 5.2.4.2]], and the limits cover the whole flight even with another pilot aboard [[36:16|AC 68-1A 5.2.5]].

steps.s: Friday you catch a head cold. At 0100 Saturday you take a nighttime cold medicine with diphenhydramine. Departure is 0900 and the weather is now fine. What now?
options: Go: it's an over-the-counter medicine and the weather is now fine
Delay until you are well and the medicine has worn off
Go, but let a pilot friend work the radios for you
Take a decongestant to clear your head, then go since you feel better
steps.why: Under a driver's license you may not fly with a condition that makes you unable to fly safely [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(b)-(c)]], or on a drug that affects your faculties [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(3)]]. Diphenhydramine causes drowsiness and lasts a long time [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].

steps.s: Two weeks later, healthy, you want to practice approaches under a view-limiting device. A friend with a private certificate (airplane single-engine land) who flies on BasicMed offers to be your safety pilot. Can she?
options: Yes, if she meets the BasicMed requirements and the flight stays within its limits
No: a safety pilot must hold an FAA medical
Only if she is also a flight instructor
Only if she acts as PIC for the flight
steps.why: The current rule lets a BasicMed pilot serve as a required flightcrew member [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)]], and a safety pilot needs at least a private certificate with the right category and class [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)(i)]]. AC 68-1A's "PIC only" line is outdated [[36:14|AC 68-1A 5.2.2.1]].

final_quiz.q: You are an ATP, 41 years old, with a first class exam dated June 20, 2026. You are scheduled as captain on a part 121 trip on January 10, 2027. Are you legal?
options: Yes: a first class lasts 12 months
No: it ended June 30, 2026
Yes, because it is still valid as a second class
No: ATP PIC privileges ended December 31, 2026
final_quiz.why: Age 40 or older at the exam: ATP PIC privileges end with the 6th month after June 2026, so December 31, 2026 [[60:208|14 CFR 61.23(d)(1)(ii)]].

final_quiz.q: Same pilot: 41 at a first class exam on June 20, 2026. Through what date does it cover commercial pilot privileges?
options: December 31, 2026
final_quiz.why: For commercial privileges a first class lasts to the end of the 12th month after the exam month at any age: June 30, 2027 [[60:208|14 CFR 61.23(d)(1)(iii)]].

final_quiz.q: A BasicMed PIC flies a 7-seat single (4,000 lb maximum takeoff weight) with 6 passengers, VFR at 9,500 ft inside the U.S. Is this legal?
options: No: too many passengers
No: too many occupants
Yes, it fits every BasicMed limit
No: BasicMed airplanes are limited to 6 seats
final_quiz.why: 7 occupants, 6 passengers and 12,500 lb are the current limits, and the altitude is well below 18,000 ft MSL [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)]].

final_quiz.q: You fly under BasicMed as PIC with a friend who holds a first class. You plan to climb to 21,000 ft for better winds, with your friend acting as PIC during that part. Legal?
options: Yes, because your friend can act as PIC during the part above 18,000 ft
No: with you as PIC the whole flight must stay within BasicMed limits
Yes, if you both use supplemental oxygen for the whole climb above 18,000 ft
Yes, if you fly it on an IFR flight plan with a clearance to 21,000 ft
final_quiz.why: If the BasicMed pilot is PIC, no portion of the flight may go beyond the limits, even if the other pilot could act as PIC outside them [[36:16|AC 68-1A 5.2.5]] [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(2)(i)]].

final_quiz.q: Your 2024 application for an FAA medical was completed and denied, and you are appealing. Your older third class from 2018 has expired. Can you use BasicMed?
options: Yes: the 2018 medical counts
Yes, once a physician completes a CMEC
Yes, while the appeal is pending
No: your most recent application was completed and denied
final_quiz.why: Your most recent application can't have been completed and denied [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)(iv)]], and you can't fall back on an older certificate or rely on an appeal [[36:11|AC 68-1A 4.3.2.1-4.3.2.2]].

final_quiz.q: A commercial pilot on BasicMed is offered $200 by a local business to fly one of its employees to a meeting. Legal?
options: Yes, because the pilot holds a commercial certificate that allows flying for pay
No: carrying a passenger for pay is a commercial privilege needing at least a second class
Yes, with one passenger on board it is well inside every BasicMed aircraft limit
Yes, if the flight is only incidental to the business that is paying the pilot $200
final_quiz.why: Commercial privileges need at least a second class [[60:204|14 CFR 61.23(a)(2)(ii)]]. Even the private business exception does not allow carrying passengers for pay [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(b)]].

final_quiz.q: Your CFI's medical expired and she doesn't use BasicMed. Which can she still do?
options: Serve as your safety pilot
Act as PIC on a discovery flight for a non-pilot
Give a flight review to a pilot who acts as PIC
Take a practical test in an airplane for a new rating
final_quiz.why: A flight instructor needs no medical when not acting as PIC or required pilot [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23(b)(7)]]. Acting as PIC, safety pilot or practical test applicant in an aircraft needs at least a third class or BasicMed [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23(a)(3)]].

final_quiz.q: Under BasicMed, which of these do you NOT need to keep?
options: Proof that you held an FAA medical after July 14, 2006
A certificate showing you completed the online course, kept in your logbook
The CMEC signed by your physician after the exam, kept in your logbook
Your U.S. driver's license, which must be in your personal possession when you fly
final_quiz.why: You need no documents proving the earlier medical [[36:12|AC 68-1A 4.3.2.3]]. The CMEC and certificate go in the logbook [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(3)]], and the license must be with you [[36:10|AC 68-1A 4.2]].

final_quiz.q: Your last drink was at 2330. You plan to depart at 0630 and feel fine. What applies?
options: Not legal: only 7 hours have passed
Legal if your blood alcohol is below 0.08
Legal, because you feel fine
Legal after 6 hours with a breath test
final_quiz.why: 2330 to 0630 is 7 hours, and 91.17 requires 8 hours after any alcohol, whatever your blood alcohol [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(1)]] [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

final_quiz.q: You hold a valid third class. You have a bad head cold but feel fine after a sedating antihistamine. What is the best answer?
options: Fly: your valid medical covers you since you feel fine
Fly, but only in daylight VFR near the airport
Don't fly: 61.53 and 91.17 apply even with a valid medical
Fly with another pilot aboard to take over
final_quiz.why: A treatment or condition that keeps you from meeting the standards grounds you [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(a)]], and so does a drug that affects your faculties [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(3)]]. Antihistamines cause drowsiness and dizziness [[1:439|PHAK 17-17]].

final_quiz.q: A BasicMed pilot is diagnosed with a neurological condition. Her specialist says it may reasonably be expected to make her unable to fly safely. What happens?
options: Nothing until her next CMEC exam
She may fly only with a safety pilot
She may fly if her family doctor signs a new CMEC
BasicMed no longer applies to her
final_quiz.why: BasicMed does not apply if the specialist judges the condition may reasonably be expected to make the pilot unable to fly safely [[60:408|14 CFR 68.9(d)(1)]] [[60:409|14 CFR 68.9(d)(1)(i)(B)]].

final_quiz.q: A student pilot flies under BasicMed. A student pilot limit in 61.89 conflicts with a BasicMed allowance in 61.113(i). Which wins?
options: The 61.89 student pilot limit
The 61.113(i) allowance
Whichever the CFI chooses
The less strict of the two
final_quiz.why: Where 61.89(a) and (b) conflict with 61.113(i), the student pilot must follow 61.89 [[60:279|14 CFR 61.89(d)]].

final_quiz.q: Your family doctor, who is not an AME, does your BasicMed exam. What must happen at that exam?
options: You give the doctor your completed CMEC section; the doctor checks every item, discusses your drugs and signs
The doctor completes and files FAA Form 8500-8 with the FAA after the exam, as for any medical
The doctor only needs to check your vision, hearing and blood pressure, then sign the checklist
The doctor must send the completed CMEC to an AME for review before you may use BasicMed
final_quiz.why: You complete your part and give it to the physician [[60:405|14 CFR 68.5(a)]]. The physician examines every listed item, discusses all drugs and signs [[60:407|14 CFR 68.7(c)]]. The doctor need not be an AME [[36:19|AC 68-1A 7.1]].
